basis: Christ's clay healing and primal formation
note: Irenaeus reads Jesus' clay healing of the man born blind as the Creator's original art of forming humanity from earth being displayed and restored. This patristic reading makes bodily formation and repair central to resurrection faith.

The Syriac Peshitta uses the cognate q-r-ʾ verb when Jesus stands to read Isaiah; this is a specific scriptural reading use beside 87:6's recitation, while the commentary's separate womb-related branch should not be transferred to this verse.

basis: childhood put away on becoming an adult
note: Paul contrasts speaking and thinking as a child with becoming an adult; this gives the commentary's child-to-maturity sequence a distinct ethical and interpretive use.
Paul explicitly asks how the dead are raised and with what sort of body they come. This names the bodily-resurrection question that the commentary raises through Q 75:40.

basis: seed must die to be made alive
note: Paul's seed analogy makes death the condition for new life; beside the commentary's embryo-to-resurrection argument and its formed-body/drying-plant pairing, it joins plant and bodily renewal.
Paul's seed image says death precedes new life. It provides a vegetal pattern for the commentary's move from a dying pasture and mortal body toward life beyond death.

basis: bare grain and body to come
note: The sower does not sow the body that will come, but a bare grain. This distinguishes initial material from its later formed body, a strong analogue to the commentary's unformed and completed stages.

basis: God gives each seed its body as willed
note: Paul says God gives each seed its own body as he wills, a close specific counterpart to the commentary's measured and specially formed body under 87:3.

basis: God gives each seed its body
note: God gives the seed a body as he chooses, to each seed its own body. The sentence makes divine assignment of bodily form an explicit resurrection counterpart to creating and proportioning.
Paul's contrast between a perishable body sown and an imperishable body raised directly answers the commentary's link between bodily creation and resurrection.
Paul contrasts a perishable sown body with an imperishable raised one. It makes the commentary's mortality-and-afterlife warning bodily and eschatological.
The body is sown in weakness and raised in power. This supplies an eschatological reversal of the frailty and declining strength that the commentary associates with old age.
Paul distinguishes the body sown as natural from the body raised as spiritual, extending the commentary's formed body and resurrection connection into a claim about transformation.
Paul distinguishes a natural body from a raised spiritual body, without discarding bodiliness. It is a useful Christian development of the commentary's body-plus-breath sequence.

basis: first Adam living soul, last Adam life-giving spirit
note: Paul interprets Genesis 2:7 by contrasting the first Adam as living soul with the last Adam as life-giving spirit; this links the commentary's formed human and breathed life to resurrection through a Christian reading of Adam.

Paul rereads Adam's becoming a living soul against the last Adam as life-giving Spirit. This Christian interpretation directly develops the formed-and-breathed human of Genesis into an eschatological body-and-life contrast.
Paul says believers will bear the image of the heavenly one. It continues his bodily-resurrection argument by moving from an earthly formed humanity toward a transformed eschatological embodiment.
John says the world and its desire pass away while the one doing God's will abides forever; this closely matches the surah's worldly-life versus better, enduring hereafter contrast.

basis: new birth through imperishable seed and word
note: Peter says his readers have been born anew through imperishable seed by God's living word; this meets the commentary's womb-and-recitation cluster and introduces a Christian new-birth image.

First Peter describes a new birth through imperishable seed and enduring word. It offers a Christian extension from bodily birth to lasting life, anticipating the flesh-and-grass contrast in the next verse.
Peter quotes Isaiah that all flesh and its glory are like grass and flower; this directly joins the commentary's mortal body and withering pasture.

First Peter quotes the formula that all flesh is like grass and its glory like a grass flower. It is the New Testament's closest verbal and conceptual counterpart to the commentary's juxtaposition of human body and withering pasture.
Peter contrasts withering flesh with the Lord's enduring word, applied to the proclaimed gospel; it develops the commentary's pasture and lasting-life contrast through Christian proclamation.

basis: new birth through resurrection to living hope
note: First Peter blesses God for giving a new birth into living hope through Jesus' resurrection. It extends the commentary's birth-and-revival nexus into a Christian account of renewed life.

At the Lord's commanding call, the dead in Christ rise first. It gives a concrete Christian scene of divine sound followed by resurrection, alongside the commentary's recitation and revivification themes.

basis: spirit, soul, and body preserved whole
note: Paul prays that spirit, soul, and body be kept whole for the Lord's coming. It is a Christian holistic counterpart to the commentary's fully ordered body and its final-life horizon.
Paul contrasts outward decay with inward renewal day by day. It makes the commentary's old-age and enduring-afterlife contrast a present bodily and spiritual discipline.
Paul contrasts what is seen and temporary with what is unseen and eternal, giving a Christian formulation of the surah's worldly-life and enduring-afterlife contrast.

basis: earthly tent and enduring divine dwelling
note: Paul contrasts the destruction of the earthly tent with an enduring dwelling from God. Its body-as-dwelling image makes the commentary's perishable worldly life and lasting future into an explicit Christian contrast.
Paul says God gives all people life, breath, and everything. It is a concise New Testament counterpart to the commentary's sequence from shaped body to enlivening breath.

Paul says God determined allotted times and the bounds of peoples' habitation. This gives a concrete New Testament use of divine determination as ordered measure, rather than an imported lexical equation.

basis: mature person and measure of fullness
note: The church's goal is mature adulthood and the measure of Christ's fullness. It takes maturity and measure into an ecclesial-ethical register, rather than describing fetal anatomy.

Paul says God set him apart from his mother's womb and called him through grace. Like Isaiah's womb-formed servant, it joins prenatal life to a directed vocation and the commentary's creation-guidance sequence.

basis: Sarah conceives beyond the age for childbearing
note: Hebrews interprets Sarah's conception as faith in the promise despite her age; beside the commentary's old-age and birth stages, it adds a Christian reading of the Genesis reversal.

basis: milk-fed child unskilled in the word
note: Hebrews likens the inexperienced hearer to an infant needing milk; this meets the commentary's child-rearing and maturation image while applying it to learning, not bodily formation.
Hebrews contrasts infants with mature people whose faculties are trained; this develops the commentary's growth-to-maturity sequence as discernment acquired over time.

basis: rich person and fading grass flower
note: James tells the rich to boast in lowliness because they pass away like a flower of grass. It closely matches the commentary's confident garden owner and the warning conveyed by worldly life and withering pasture.

basis: sun scorches grass and beauty perishes
note: James completes the image: sun scorches the grass, its flower falls, and the rich fade in their pursuits. This gives the image an ethical warning about transient prosperity, as in the commentary's ruined garden.

basis: life as a briefly appearing vapor
note: James describes present life as vapor that appears briefly and vanishes. It provides a compact ethical analogue to the commentary's warning that worldly life and its flourishing are transient.

basis: birth brings a child into the world and ends remembered anguish
note: Jesus compares the disciples' sorrow to labor pain that gives way to joy when a child is born into the world; this meets the commentary's delivery-nearness sense for al-dunya and its womb-related reading of qaraʾ, without claiming either Arabic branch as the verse's literal meaning.

Nicodemus hears new birth in literal bodily terms and asks about entering a mother's womb a second time. The question exposes the bodily reading that the following saying redirects, creating a useful contrast with the commentary's literal fetal imagery.

Jesus answers the womb question with birth from water and Spirit. It reworks birth imagery toward eschatological renewal, a Christian counter-reading to place beside the commentary's body-and-breath account.

basis: those in tombs hear the voice
note: Jesus says all who are in tombs will hear his voice. It supplies a New Testament voice-to-bodily-resurrection counterpart to the commentary's move from divine speech and formation to the raising of the dead.
Those who hear come out, to life or judgment according to their deeds. The bodily emergence and divided final outcome develop the resurrection horizon invoked by the commentary.

John is said to be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother's womb. It makes the womb a site of divine life and vocation, a specific New Testament counterpart to the commentary's prenatal life imagery.
The angel says Elizabeth, called barren, is now six months pregnant in her old age; this precisely brings the commentary's old-age and approaching-birth senses into one Christian narrative.
At Mary's greeting, the infant leaps in Elizabeth's womb; this adds a concrete action of the fetus within the womb to the commentary's prenatal life-stage imagery.
At Mary's greeting, the child leaps in Elizabeth's womb. The narrative gives a concrete fetal bodily response to divine visitation, rather than an abstract use of womb language.

basis: life required from the storing rich man
note: God tells the rich planner that his life is demanded that night. The sudden end to stored abundance is a close ethical meeting with the commentary's garden owner who trusts worldly security before it vanishes.
Luke describes Jesus growing as a child, becoming strong and filled with wisdom; it supplies a concrete growth-to-maturity scene for the commentary's Rabb-as-child-rearing branch.

basis: Jesus advances in age and stature
note: Jesus increases in wisdom, stature, and favor; this is a direct bodily-growth counterpart to the commentary's reading of maturation through a human life.

basis: growth in wisdom, stature, and favor
note: Jesus advances in wisdom, stature, and favor. It is a concise New Testament life-stage counterpart to the commentary's sense of reaching full youth and ordered maturation.

basis: resurrected people can no longer die
note: In Jesus' reply about the resurrection, those deemed worthy of that age can no longer die; this gives a Christian contrast to the surah's condemned who neither die nor live.

The earth yields first a stalk, then an ear, then full grain; this plant-growth sequence meets the commentary's child-raised-in-stages and pasture imagery while remaining an agrarian, not human, account.
The ripe crop is harvested, completing Mark's growth sequence; beside the commentary's vegetation growth and drying, it adds the endpoint of maturity and harvest.
Jesus asks what profit it is to gain the whole world and lose one's life; this states explicitly the danger implicit in the commentary's identification of preferring worldly life.

basis: Gehenna's worm does not die and fire is not quenched
note: Jesus uses Isaiah's undying-worm and unquenched-fire image as a warning about Gehenna; beside the surah's great fire and its continuation that the condemned neither die nor live, it gives a Christian judgment image with a different formulation.
Jesus contrasts earthly treasure vulnerable to decay with treasure secured in heaven; this gives a concrete image to the surah's preference for worldly life over what is better and enduring.

basis: no one can add a cubit to stature or lifespan
note: Jesus asks whether anxiety can add a cubit to a person's ἡλικία, read as stature or lifespan; this specific ambiguity meets the commentary's measured body and measured human course.

Jesus asks which anxious person can add a span to life. This is a focused New Testament counterpart to the commentary's measured human lifespan, with a warning against investing trust in present life.

basis: field grass clothed today, burned tomorrow
note: Jesus says God clothes grass that is thrown into the oven the next day; the image joins the commentary's pasture that withers to bodily care and fire, while Matthew's point is trust rather than judgment.

Jesus describes grass alive today and thrown into an oven tomorrow while arguing for divine care. The image links bodily concern and transient grass, though its immediate point is anxiety rather than resurrection.

Paul says Christ will transform the body of humiliation to conform to his glorious body; this is a direct Christian counterpart to the commentary's ordered body and resurrection, with transformation rather than mere return.
Christ will transform the body of lowliness to conform to his glorious body. The verse gives a specifically Christian answer to the commentary's movement from mortal formed body to life after death.

basis: people seek death, but death flees
note: During the locust torment, people desire death without finding it; this concretely meets the surah's adjacent statement that those in the fire neither die nor live, although Revelation's torment scene is not itself the final lake of fire.

basis: gives life to dead and calls what is not
note: Paul characterizes God as giving life to the dead and calling into being things that are not. The paired creation-and-revival formula closely matches the commentary's use of fetal creation as evidence for resurrection.

basis: Spirit gives life to mortal bodies
note: The Spirit who raised Jesus will give life to mortal bodies. It directly joins divine indwelling spirit, bodily mortality, and resurrection in the way the commentary connects formation, breath, and revivification.
Paul pictures all creation groaning in labor pains; this brings the commentary's womb-centered bodily life cycle into a cosmic creation image.

Paul figures the whole creation as groaning together in childbirth. The verse applies labor imagery to creation's movement toward redemption, an interpretive extension of the commentary's body, earth, and resurrection linkage.
Believers groan while awaiting bodily redemption; this connects the commentary's formed human body and resurrection argument with Paul's future transformation of the body.

basis: martyr expects to receive his limbs again
note: A tortured brother says he received his limbs from heaven and hopes to receive them again; this Jewish witness makes resurrection bodily and specific, beside the commentary's inference from bodily creation to raising the dead.

basis: king has no resurrection to life
note: The youngest brother expects God to raise him to life, while the king has no resurrection to life; this adds the commentary's bodily revival theme together with opposed postmortem destinies.

The mother of the martyrs says she does not know how her children came to be in her womb and denies that she gave them life or set their elements in order. It closely mirrors the commentary's created, ordered fetus while locating agency in the Creator.

The mother says the Creator will return life and breath to her sons. The verse directly makes prenatal formation an argument for resurrection, exactly the inferential move foregrounded by the commentary.
The mother points to heaven, earth, and the human race as made by God. In her martyrdom context this supports hope beyond death, extending the commentary's creation-to-resurrection reasoning.

basis: dust-made body and breath of life
note: Fourth Ezra says God commanded dust to give Adam, a lifeless body formed by divine hands, then breathed life into him. The retelling explicitly combines the commentary's earth, fashioned body, and breath sequence.

basis: formed in wisdom; openings and cavities
note: The Asher Yatzar blessing praises the one who formed the human in wisdom with openings and cavities whose proper functioning sustains life. It offers a Jewish liturgical analogue to the commentary's well-proportioned, disease-free body ordered by wisdom.

basis: origin in a drop; return to dust
note: Avot asks a person to remember the bodily origin in a drop and the destination of dust and decay. Its ethical memento turns the life-course images of the commentary into a warning against worldly self-assurance.

basis: formed, born, lives, dies, and gives account
note: Avot presents human formation, birth, life, death, and judgment as an involuntary ordered sequence. It is a rabbinic whole-life formulation for the stages the commentary assembles from womb to old age and final reckoning.

basis: fetus taught Torah, then made to forget
note: The Talmud says an angel teaches the fetus Torah in the womb and strikes it at birth so it forgets; this meets the commentary's womb association for the root of 87:6 with that verse's recitation and not-forgetting, while the Talmud's fetus and Qur'anic addressee differ.

basis: fetus in womb taught Torah then made to forget
note: Niddah says the fetus is taught Torah in the womb and an angel causes it to forget at birth. The combination of womb, instruction, and forgetting is a specific meeting with Q 87:6's recitation and not-forgetting beside the commentary's womb sense for its root.

basis: parents' material and God's life-giving share
note: The Talmud distinguishes parental contributions to bones, flesh, and other features from God's gift of spirit, soul, senses, and understanding. It is a detailed Jewish account of an ordered body joined to life and capacity.

Rabbi Meir answers a question about resurrection by pointing to grain buried bare that emerges clothed; this Jewish argument uses plant transformation to make renewed embodiment imaginable, meeting the commentary's pairing of bodily creation, resurrection, and vegetation.

basis: grain buried and clothed in rising
note: Rabbi Meir answers a resurrection question with wheat that is buried bare and emerges clothed. The rabbinic analogy joins vegetal renewal to bodily resurrection, like the commentary's body-and-pasture pairing.

Sirach describes the Lord assigning created works their portions and arranging them in order. It is a Jewish development of the commentary's claim that each thing is put in a particular measure and mode.

basis: human from earth and returned to it
note: Sirach says the Lord created humans from earth and lets them return to it. It adds a sapiential version of the soil-to-body-to-death arc underlying the commentary's resurrection reflection.

Sirach attributes human tongue, eyes, ears, mind, knowledge, and understanding to God. It offers a sapiential expansion of the commentary's properly ordered body into its sensory and cognitive capacities.

basis: from leaving the womb to returning to the mother of all living
note: Sirach describes human toil as spanning birth from the womb to return to earth, an unusually explicit lifespan parallel to the commentary's womb-to-aging sequence.

basis: from mother's womb to return to earth
note: Sirach frames the human burden from leaving the mother's womb until returning to the mother of all. It explicitly spans the bodily life course from birth to death that the commentary assembles from its roots.

Onkelos renders the human made living in Genesis as a speaking spirit. That interpretive rendering links the formed and breathed body to speech, which helps place Q 87:6's recitation beside the commentary's bodily reading of its root.

basis: living soul rendered as speaking spirit
note: Onqelos interprets the formed human's life-breath as a speaking spirit; this Jewish reading connects the bodily formation discussed for 87:2 with the surah's adjacent gift of recitation in 87:6.

basis: sleepers in dust awake to opposed destinies
note: Daniel says many sleeping in the dust awake to everlasting life or shame; this gives a Hebrew Bible resurrection counterpart to the commentary's creation-to-resurrection argument and places judgment after bodily renewal.
Daniel depicts many sleeping in earth's dust awakening to divergent lasting destinies. It gives the eschatological endpoint of the commentary's earth-to-body-to-resurrection arc.

basis: Israel forgets the God who gave it birth
note: Moses accuses Israel of forgetting the God who gave it birth; this meets the commentary's womb and child-raising senses beside 87:6's promise not to forget, but reverses the roles: Israel forgets its divine parent.

basis: bones formed in a pregnant woman's womb
note: Ecclesiastes contrasts the unknown formation of bones in the womb with God's work as maker of all; this directly joins the commentary's fetal body-shaping and divine ordering, while stressing that the process is hidden.

Ecclesiastes invokes the formation of bones in a pregnant woman as something humans do not know, then extends that ignorance to God's work. It checks any attempt to turn the commentary's lexical fetal images into a claimed account of fetal mechanics.

basis: remember the Creator before aging days
note: Ecclesiastes urges remembrance of the Creator before difficult years and old age arrive, joining the commentary's Creator-centered bodily life course to its age-related reading.

basis: remember Creator in days of youth
note: Ecclesiastes calls for remembering the Creator during youth before the difficult days arrive. It makes youth and later decline an ethical frame, matching the commentary's use of completed youth and old age as life stages.
The poem pictures trembling hands, bent strength, failing teeth, and dim eyes; it gives physical detail to the commentary's otherwise brief old-age sense.

basis: fear of heights and journey to the eternal home
note: The old-age poem moves from bodily frailty to the human going to an eternal home, adding the life's endpoint to the commentary's aging stage.

At death, dust returns to earth and spirit to God; this reverses the dust-and-breath formation of Genesis 2:7 and supplies an endpoint to the commentary's bodily lifespan, without itself arguing for resurrection.

basis: dust returns; spirit returns to God
note: Ecclesiastes separates the body's return to earth from the spirit's return to God. It gives a sharply stated deathward counterpart to the commentary's body-and-breath account and its afterlife horizon.

basis: time to be born and time to die
note: Ecclesiastes frames human life with a time for birth and a time for death, a concise lifespan formula beside the commentary's womb-to-old-age reading.

basis: newborn with cord uncut, unwashed, and unswaddled
note: The commentary's camel idiom mentions fetal membranes not gathered; Ezekiel's allegory depicts a newborn left with its cord uncut and without birth care. The objects differ, but both make perinatal handling concrete.

basis: the breath enters and the slain live
note: The bodies stand alive after the breath enters them; this is a vivid resurrection-like image beside the commentary's argument from bodily formation to God's power to raise the dead, though Ezekiel interprets the vision corporately.

basis: breath gives life to assembled bodies
note: Once breath enters, the assembled bodies live and stand. The verse completes the formation-to-life sequence that the commentary traces from fetal body to resurrection.
God promises to put his spirit within the people so that they live. Its own national-restoration setting makes the bodily image an interpretive rather than a simple individual-resurrection equation.

In Ezekiel's vision God promises breath to dry bones so that they will live. It supplies an explicit bodily-revival analogue for the commentary's citation of embryonic creation as evidence for raising the dead.

basis: sinews, flesh, skin, and breath restore a body
note: In a vision interpreted as Israel's restoration (37:11), God reassembles the dry bones with bodily tissues and breath; this supplies a detailed scriptural image of the ordered body and renewed life discussed in the commentary.

God orders sinews, flesh, skin, and breath onto bones. The ordered rebuilding of a body is a close counterpart to formed flesh, bodily proportion, and later life; Ezekiel's own vision then identifies this with Israel's restoration.

basis: body assembled but still without breath
note: The bones have sinews, flesh, and skin, yet no breath; this makes bodily formation and animation distinct stages, sharpening the commentary's creation-and-order sequence.

basis: breath summoned from the four winds to the slain
note: The prophet is told to call breath into the slain so they may live; this joins the commentary's formed body with divine breath and revival, in a vision whose stated referent is exiled Israel.

Hebrew rabah, to become many, is a cognate family relevant to the commentary's source label r-b-b. Genesis uses it for human fruitfulness and multiplication, not for the Arabic sense of rearing a child stage by stage.

basis: Sarah and Abraham advanced in age; her monthly cycle had ceased
note: The narrative names the aged body's reproductive limit before Isaac's promised birth, bringing the commentary's old-age and approaching-birth stages together in one concrete case.

basis: Hebrew qara, calling names after formation
note: Hebrew qara, to call or name, belongs to the Semitic q-r-ʾ family also heard in Q 87:6's recitation verb. Here Adam names creatures after their formation, so it supports speech after creation but does not carry the commentary's Arabic womb-closure sense.
The commentary reads 87:2's creating and proportioning bodily; Genesis narrates God forming the first human from ground and breathing life into him, adding the dust-to-living-body sequence.

Genesis forms the human from ground and then gives life by divine breath. It provides a close biblical sequence for the commentary's ordered body and its cited Q 32:9 breath, while retaining an earthly material origin.

basis: Sarah conceives and bears Isaac in old age
note: Isaac is born to Sarah at the time God promised, when Abraham is old; this gives a narrative reversal in which the commentary's late-life stage becomes the setting for birth.

basis: Sarah nurses a son in Abraham's old age
note: Sarah marvels that she has borne and nursed a son in Abraham's old age; this uniquely combines the commentary's child-rearing and senescence stages.

After the human is taken from the ground, God says he will return to it; this completes the earth-to-body sequence cited in the commentary with its bodily endpoint before the Qur'anic resurrection argument.
The human formed from ground is told to return to dust. It supplies the deathward side of the commentary's earth, body, and resurrection sequence, though it does not itself promise revival.

basis: taught Ephraim to walk and lifted him by the arms
note: God recalls teaching Israel as a child to walk and carrying him; this is a concrete child-rearing scene for the commentary's Rabb-as-raising-a-child sense.

basis: lifted infant and bent down to feed
note: God describes lifting Israel like an infant and bending down to feed him; this extends the commentary's nurturing life-stage image into hands-on parental care.

basis: dead awaken and earth gives birth to shades
note: Isaiah calls the dead to live and the earth to give birth to its dead; this joins bodily resurrection to birth imagery, meeting the commentary's fetal formation and resurrection argument.

basis: earth gives birth to the dead
note: Isaiah calls sleepers in dust to awake and portrays earth as giving birth to the dead. The birth image makes an especially close counterpart to the commentary's inference from prenatal formation to resurrection.
Isaiah identifies all flesh with grass and its glory with a field flower; this makes the commentary's pairing of human body and drying pasture an explicit image of mortality.
Isaiah's voice calls all flesh grass and human constancy a field flower. The explicit flesh-and-grass equation strongly parallels the commentary's body and drying pasture as two faces of one warning.
Grass withers and the flower fades when the Lord's breath blows on it. It adds the agency of divine breath to the commentary's life-and-pasture contrast.

Isaiah contrasts withering grass and fading flowers with God's enduring word; beside the surah's dried pasture and its enduring-afterlife contrast, it adds a biblical word-versus-mortal-life formulation.

basis: breath to people and spirit to walkers
note: Isaiah's creator gives breath to the people on earth and spirit to those who walk on it. This is a compact creation-and-life formulation alongside the commentary's Q 32:9 comparison.
Isaiah names the Lord as both maker and one who forms the addressee from the womb. This directly joins the two creation verbs that the commentary develops as fetal formation.

basis: Creator says he formed Israel from the womb
note: Isaiah joins forming the addressee in the womb to the Lord's making of all things; this ties the commentary's prenatal formation directly to universal creation.

The speaker again identifies himself as maker of all and former of the addressee from the womb. Its cosmic and prenatal scopes together illuminate the commentary's claim that a measured human body belongs to a larger created order.
God says he has borne and carried Israel from the womb; this makes the commentary's Rabb-as-raising image a lifelong divine-care metaphor, though Isaiah speaks collectively of Israel.
God addresses those carried from the belly and borne from the womb. It begins a divine care sequence at prenatal and birth stages, matching the commentary's life-course reading.
The same oracle promises to carry Israel into old age and gray hairs, bringing the commentary's womb-to-senescence life arc under one image of divine care.

basis: until old age and gray hair
note: The same divine bearer remains present until old age and gray hair. This is a particularly exact lifespan counterpart to the commentary's movement from the womb through maturity to senescence.
Isaiah asks whether a mother can forget the son of her womb, then says God will not forget Zion; this meets the commentary's womb, nurture, and not-forgetting cluster through a maternal-memory image.
The servant says the Lord formed him from the womb for service. It joins bodily formation to calling, a useful counterpart both to Q 87:2's formation and to the recited commission in Q 87:6.
Isaiah calls a mortal human being like grass. This directly joins the human body and fading vegetation that the commentary treats as one warning about temporary worldly life.

basis: spirit and breath made by God
note: Isaiah says that the spirit would fail before God, along with the breaths God has made. The verse joins creaturely frailty with divine authorship of breath, though its immediate context is divine restraint from wrath.

Isaiah's closing vision has worshipers view the corpses of rebels with undying worms and unquenched fire; beside 87:12–13, it shares fire and undying imagery but depicts corpses rather than living people unable to die.

basis: formed in womb before prophetic commission
note: Jeremiah is known and set apart before being formed in the womb; this shares the commentary's divine prenatal formation while adding vocation before birth.

basis: formed, known, and appointed before birth
note: Jeremiah is known before womb-formation and appointed before emergence. The verse makes divine formation part of a life directed toward a purpose, sharpening the commentary's measure-and-guidance claim.

basis: from mother's womb to naked return
note: Job says he came naked from his mother's womb and will return naked. The saying compresses bodily origin and mortality into the life-course arc that the commentary traces from womb formation to its end.
Job pictures his own formation in the womb as milk becoming cheese; this gives concrete gestational process to the commentary's fetal-forming life-stage reading.
Job figures his prenatal making as liquid poured like milk and curdled like cheese. That material, staged image belongs beside the commentary's formed and unformed embryonic body.
Job says God clothed and knit these body parts together, closely specifying the bodily ordering that the commentary hears in 87:2–3.

Job describes being clothed with skin and flesh and woven with bones and sinews. It is a concrete bodily counterpart to the commentary's claim that creation and setting right can be heard as bodily formation.

After the anatomical images, Job says God granted life and guarded his spirit. It joins formed flesh to a divinely sustained life, as the commentary joins proportioning to breath and eventual revivification.
Job addresses God as the maker who fashioned and made him, a personal bodily counterpart to the commentary's account of creation and arrangement.

Job says God's hands fashioned him all around, then protests that the same maker turns to destroy him. The shared embodied formation is set in a lament, a deliberate tension with the praise of creating and proportioning in Q 87:2.

basis: human born of woman, brief as a fading flower
note: Job joins birth from a woman to a short life that flowers and withers; this connects the commentary's lifespan arc to its body-and-drying-vegetation warning.

basis: Job asks whether a dead person will live again
note: Job asks whether a human who dies will live again and says he would wait for release; this places the commentary's confident move from bodily formation to resurrection beside a Hebrew lament that frames renewed life as a question and hope.
Job says a person's days are determined, months numbered, and limit set; this closely meets the commentary's reading of 87:3 as assigning each thing its measure, here applied to human lifespan.
Job says a person's days and months are determined and bounded by God. This directly supplies the temporal side of the commentary's particular measure (qaddara) across a human life.

basis: one maker fashioned both people in the womb
note: Job grounds equality between himself and his servant in the same maker forming them in the womb; this adds an ethical consequence to the commentary's account of shared human bodily formation.
Job grounds equal human standing in one maker who made both people in the womb and fashioned them there. The shared point is divine womb-formation, not merely a general creator title.

basis: Spirit made me; breath gives life
note: Job's interlocutor says God's Spirit made him and the Almighty's breath gives him life. It is a particularly direct Hebrew Bible counterpart to the commentary's formed body followed by enlivening breath.
Elihu imagines God gathering back to himself a creature's spirit and breath. This supplies the withdrawal side of the commentary's body-and-breath sequence.

basis: all flesh perishes and returns to dust
note: The consequence of withdrawn breath is that all flesh dies and humanity returns to dust. It makes the body, breath, and earth sequence explicit before any resurrection answer is supplied.

Job calls God kabbir, great or mighty, a cognate family of Arabic kabir. The Hebrew context keeps greatness rather than age in view, which helps distinguish the commentary's age-related Arabic root note from the actual 'great' fire of Q 87:12.
Proverbs contrasts young men's strength with gray hair as elders' splendor, giving a compact scriptural life-stage pair beside the commentary's maturity and senescence readings.

basis: God knows the frame and remembers dust
note: The psalm says God knows the human frame and remembers that humans are dust. It ties bodily construction to earthly frailty, supplementing the commentary's formed body and its eventual decline.

basis: human days like grass and field flower
note: The psalm compares human days and flourishing to grass and a flower, directly joining bodily lifespan to vegetation as the commentary does in its life-stage and pasture reading.

The psalm explicitly compares a human's days to grass and a flowering field. It closely matches the commentary's pairing of the ordered body with the pasture that dries up as one warning about mortal life.
The flower disappears when wind passes; this adds the disappearance of mortal life to the commentary's warning carried by drying pasture.
The following verse makes the grass vanish when the wind passes over it. It supplies the disappearance that gives the body-and-pasture comparison its warning force.
When God takes away breath, living creatures die and return to dust. This links breath, bodily mortality, and earth in the same sequence the commentary connects to creation and resurrection.

God sends breath, creatures are created, and the ground is renewed. The verse places animate creation and revived earth together, paralleling the commentary's juxtaposition of body and watered pasture.

basis: hands made and fashioned; request for understanding
note: The psalmist says divine hands made and fashioned him, then asks for understanding of commandments. It brings formed person and divinely directed understanding together, bridging Q 87:2-3's creation and guidance.
The psalmist credits God with forming inward parts and knitting him in his mother's womb, making explicit the prenatal bodily scene behind the commentary's life-stage reading.
The psalm attributes the inward parts and covering in the mother's womb to God. It is a direct counterpart to the commentary's womb enclosure and fetal bodily formation.
The psalm's hidden, intricately woven formation in the body's depths adds a concealed-making image to the commentary's womb and shaping sequence.
The speaker's frame is made in secret and woven in hidden depths. Its hidden craftsmanship gives a biblical form to the commentary's transition from unformed to fully shaped body.
The psalm joins an embryo not yet formed to days written beforehand; it brings prenatal formation together with the measured lifespan heard in the commentary's qaḍara and life-cycle reading.

God sees the speaker's unformed substance, and the days are written before they arrive. The verse combines embryo imagery with a measured lifespan, the two strands of the commentary's reading of created and apportioned life.

basis: measure of days and life's end
note: The psalm asks God to make known the measure of its days and its end; this makes the commentary's measured-life reading of 87:3 a prayer about human limits.
The psalmist asks to know the measure and extent of his days. This gives a personal, prayerful analogue to the commentary's understanding of qaddara as a life set to a measure.

basis: God relied on from the womb
note: The speaker says God has been his hope from birth and benefactor from the womb, an individual prayer counterpart to the commentary's nurturing life-cycle sense of Rabb.
The psalmist places dependence on God from the mother's belly onward. Together with its old-age plea, it gives the lifespan arc that the commentary hears in child-rearing and senescence.
The psalmist asks not to be abandoned in old age; this makes the commentary's senescence sense concrete as a prayer about divine care at life's late stage.
The same speaker asks not to be abandoned in old age when strength fails. This is a specific biblical counterpart to the commentary's move from fetal formation through maturity toward old age.
The psalm assigns human life seventy or, at strength, eighty years, then says it passes swiftly; this makes the commentary's measured-body and old-age senses an explicit lifespan measure.
The psalm asks God to teach people to number their days; it joins the commentary's measured lifespan to the guidance of 87:3, with numbering leading to wise living.

basis: fruitful and green in old age
note: The righteous remain fruitful, fresh, and green in old age; the verse uniquely joins the commentary's aging body with its surah's pasture and vegetation imagery.

basis: all things ordered by measure, number, and weight
note: Wisdom says God ordered all things by measure, number, and weight; this closely specifies the commentary's reading of 87:3 as putting each thing in its particular measure and form.

Wisdom says God arranged all things by measure, number, and weight. This is an unusually exact Jewish formulation of the commentary's account of qaddara as placing each thing in a particular measure and form.

basis: power over life, death, and return
note: Wisdom attributes authority over life and death to God, including bringing people down to Hades and back. It is a direct Jewish formulation of the creation-to-resurrection inference developed in the commentary.

Wisdom says God created humanity for incorruption and made it in the likeness of divine eternity. It gives a Jewish counterweight to bodily decay that closely matches the commentary's contrast of worldly life with what endures.
Solomon presents himself as mortal and descended from the first human formed from earth; this places the commentary's bodily ordering within a Jewish reflection on universal human origin.

basis: molded into flesh in mother's womb
note: Wisdom's speaker says he was molded into flesh in a mother's womb. It is a late Jewish, explicitly prenatal formulation of the bodily shaping developed in the commentary.
Solomon describes being molded in flesh in his mother's womb over ten months, a direct gestational counterpart to the commentary's fetal formation.
The next verse describes gestation in a fixed period and bodily material from seed and blood. Its timed, material account closely meets the commentary's womb gathering and measured formation.
The infant receives breath and cries at birth; it extends the commentary's prenatal-to-lifespan sequence across the body's emergence from the womb.
The speaker moves from womb formation to birth and breathing the common air. That transition is useful beside the commentary's formed body followed by divine breath and life.
Solomon says he was swaddled and cared for, giving a concrete childhood instance of the commentary's branch of Rabb as raising a child.
Even a king's birth has no different beginning; this Jewish reflection makes the commentary's bodily life stages universal rather than a lexical claim about one person.
All people share one way into life and one way out; it frames the commentary's womb-to-old-age arc with mortality and a common human course.
